---
title: "From prices to simulated paths"
---

## 1. Generate a toy price history

This report uses a five-year synthetic series generated with a known GBM process. It is intentionally simple and deterministic, so rendering the document produces the same example each time.

```{python}
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "src")

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from market_demo import generate_prices, log_returns, estimate_parameters, simulate_gbm

prices = generate_prices()
returns = log_returns(prices)
```

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))
ax.plot(prices.index, prices, color="#2878B5", linewidth=1.3)
ax.set(title="Synthetic daily closing price", xlabel="Date", ylabel="Price")
ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
print(f"Starting price: {prices.iloc[0]:.2f}")
print(f"Ending price:   {prices.iloc[-1]:.2f}")
```

This is one random realization, not a claim about how a real asset behaves.

## 2. Calculate and inspect log returns

For consecutive prices (P_t), the continuously compounded return is \[ r_t = \log(P_t) - \log(P\_{t-1}). \] Log returns are additive over time and are a convenient input for this illustrative GBM calibration.

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
axes[0].plot(returns.index, returns, color="#59A14F", linewidth=0.65)
axes[0].set(title="Daily log returns", xlabel="Date", ylabel="Return")
axes[0].axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.7)
axes[1].hist(returns, bins=45, density=True, color="#59A14F", alpha=0.75)
axes[1].set(title="Return distribution", xlabel="Daily log return", ylabel="Density")
for ax in axes:
    ax.grid(alpha=0.2)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The histogram is descriptive, not a formal goodness-of-fit test. A real financial return series may have heavier tails, volatility clustering, and other features this toy model does not represent.

## 3. Calibrate annualized parameters

The sample standard deviation of daily log returns is scaled by (\sqrt{252}). The drift estimate converts the average daily log return to an annualized GBM drift by adding half the estimated annual variance.

```{python}
estimates = estimate_parameters(returns)
print(f"Estimated annualized drift:      {estimates['drift']:.1%}")
print(f"Estimated annualized volatility: {estimates['volatility']:.1%}")
```

## 4. Simulate and compare

Use those estimates to simulate paths over the same number of trading days. The median and 5th–95th percentile band summarize the simulated paths; they are not a confidence interval for a real asset.

```{python}
paths = simulate_gbm(
    initial_price=float(prices.iloc[0]),
    n_days=len(returns),
    drift=estimates["drift"],
    volatility=estimates["volatility"],
)
simulated_median = paths.median(axis=1)
lower = paths.quantile(0.05, axis=1)
upper = paths.quantile(0.95, axis=1)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.5))
ax.plot(range(len(prices)), prices.to_numpy(), color="#2878B5", linewidth=1.4, label="Synthetic history")
ax.fill_between(paths.index, lower, upper, color="#F28E2B", alpha=0.2, label="Simulated 5th–95th percentile")
ax.plot(paths.index, simulated_median, color="#E15759", linewidth=1.4, label="Simulated median")
ax.set(title="Observed synthetic path and calibrated GBM paths", xlabel="Trading day", ylabel="Price")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Takeaway

This is the simplest useful workflow, not a production model: a seeded synthetic dataset, a transparent estimator, a simulation, and plots that explain each step. The Python functions live in `src/market_demo.py`, so the same calculations can be reused in a notebook, report, or another tool.
